description: Explore UK health campaigns, their methods, and how to judge whether they work.

content_html:
Current UK Health Campaigns

The specification requires students to know named, current UK health campaigns across a range of themes. Exam questions often ask students to “name a current campaign” or “give an example of a campaign that promotes [specific health behaviour]” — a vague answer like “a healthy eating campaign” will not score marks. The campaigns below are grouped by theme, as they appear in the specification, and reflect initiatives that are active in the 2025–26 academic year. Note that campaign names change: Change4Life (now NHS Better Health) is one such example — students should know both names.

Campaigns by Theme

Alcohol awareness: Dry January (Alcohol Change UK) runs every January and encourages participants to abstain from alcohol for the month. It has grown significantly since its launch in 2013, with millions of participants annually. Research consistently shows short-term improvements in liver function, blood pressure and sleep quality among participants.

Smoking cessation: No Smoking Day is an annual awareness day held each March, raising awareness of the harms of smoking and signposting support services including NHS Stop Smoking services. It has been running since 1984. Stoptober runs each October and encourages smokers to quit for the month of October, with evidence that those who stop for 28 days are five times more likely to quit for good.

Men’s health: Movember takes place every November, targeting men’s health issues including prostate cancer, testicular cancer, and men’s mental health. By focusing on a visible and engaging activity (sponsored moustache-growing), it reaches men who might not otherwise engage with health services.

Mental health: Time to Talk Day is held each February and is run jointly by Mind and Rethink Mental Illness. It encourages people to have conversations about mental health to reduce stigma and encourage help-seeking. Five Ways to Well-being was developed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) for the government and has been widely adopted by NHS and local authority well-being programmes. The five actions are: connect (with people around you), be active, take notice (of the world around you), keep learning, and give (to others).

Physical activity: Cycle to Work Day encourages employees to cycle to work as a healthy and sustainable commuting choice. It is run in partnership with employers and local authorities. This Girl Can (Sport England) uses authentic, diverse imagery to encourage women and girls to be physically active regardless of their fitness level or body shape, specifically addressing the barriers of self-consciousness and fear of judgement.

Community health and safety: Anti-Bullying Week takes place each November, run by the Anti-Bullying Alliance, promoting positive relationships in schools and online. Keeping Warm in Winter campaigns (coordinated by NHS and local councils) target older adults and those with chronic conditions, reducing the health risks of cold homes including respiratory illness and cardiovascular events. Catch It, Bin It, Kill It is a long-running respiratory hygiene campaign reminding people to catch sneezes and coughs in a tissue and dispose of it promptly, reducing the spread of respiratory infections.

Key Fact

Current named campaigns include: Dry January (alcohol); No Smoking Day and Stoptober (smoking); Movember (men’s health); Time to Talk Day and Five Ways to Well-being (mental health); Cycle to Work Day and This Girl Can (physical activity); Anti-Bullying Week (community). Knowing the campaign name, its theme, and one key feature is the minimum required to score marks.

Methods Used to Deliver Health Campaigns

The specification identifies six main methods through which health campaigns reach their audiences. Understanding each method allows students to evaluate how campaigns are delivered and to assess their likely effectiveness for different target groups.

1. Printed materials (leaflets and posters): Traditional and cost-effective. Leaflets in GP surgeries, pharmacies and community centres reach people at moments when they may be thinking about their health. Posters in public spaces (bus stops, schools, workplaces) build repeated exposure to a message. Limitation: can be ignored, may not reach those with low literacy.

2. Websites and online resources: The NHS and campaign organisations maintain websites with in-depth information, self-assessment tools, and signposting to support services. Websites allow people to access information privately, at a time of their choosing. Limitation: depends on internet access and digital literacy, which are not universal.

3. Television advertisements: Reach a mass audience quickly and can use emotional storytelling to change attitudes. NHS campaigns (including anti-smoking and mental health awareness) have used TV advertising effectively. Limitation: expensive to produce; audiences can skip or tune out.

4. Celebrities, soap operas and drama: Storylines in popular soap operas (such as EastEnders and Emmerdale) have addressed topics including domestic abuse, cancer diagnosis, addiction, and dementia, raising awareness among audiences who might not actively seek health information. Celebrity involvement in campaigns (such as sportspeople promoting exercise or mental health advocates speaking publicly) increases reach and relatability. Limitation: entertainment content is not always factually accurate.

5. Social media, internet and pop-ups: Social media platforms allow campaigns to reach specific demographic groups with targeted messaging. Movember and Time to Talk Day both use social media to encourage sharing and peer-to-peer advocacy. Pop-up adverts on websites and apps can target individuals based on search behaviour. Limitation: algorithm-driven platforms may not reach those most in need; misinformation spreads rapidly online.

6. Guest speakers in schools and colleges: A health professional, service user or campaign representative speaking directly to young people can be more impactful than printed materials, because it allows for questions, personal testimony and two-way dialogue. Limitation: resource-intensive; effectiveness depends heavily on the quality of the speaker and session.

Key Fact

The six delivery methods are: printed materials (leaflets, posters); websites; television advertisements; celebrities and soap operas; social media and internet pop-ups; guest speakers in schools and colleges. Each method has different reach, cost, and effectiveness for different target groups.

Reliability and Validity of Health Campaign Information

Not all health information is equally trustworthy. A key skill in health and social care is being able to assess whether information is reliable (consistent, produced by a credible organisation, confirmed by other sources) and valid (accurate, based on sound evidence, and appropriate for the individual).

When evaluating a health campaign, students should consider: who produced the information (is it an NHS body, a recognised charity such as Mind or Cancer Research UK, or a commercial organisation with a financial interest?); what evidence underpins the claims (is it peer-reviewed research, or anecdote?); when it was produced (health guidance changes as new evidence emerges; an older campaign may contain outdated advice); and whether it is appropriate for the target group (a campaign aimed at young men that uses text-heavy leaflets may be less effective than a video on social media).

Compare two sources of information about stopping smoking. Source A is an NHS Better Health Stop Smoking page, citing clinical trials showing the effectiveness of nicotine replacement therapy, updated in 2024 and reviewed by NHS medical advisers. Source B is a blog post by a supplement company recommending a proprietary product to “curb nicotine cravings naturally”, with testimonials but no clinical citations. Source A is more reliable: it is produced by a public health body with no commercial interest, is based on peer-reviewed clinical evidence, and is regularly updated. Source B has lower reliability: the producer has a commercial interest in selling a product, and the evidence is anecdotal rather than clinical. In a care setting, only Source A would be appropriate to share with a service user who wants to stop smoking.
exam_tip_html: Exam questions on campaigns often ask you to ‘name’ or ‘identify’ a current health campaign — always give the specific name (e.g. Dry January, not just “an alcohol awareness campaign”). For questions about reliability and validity, avoid vague answers like “I would check it is from a good source”. Be specific: name the type of organisation (e.g. NHS, registered charity, government body), the type of evidence (clinical trials rather than testimonials), and the currency of the information (recently updated rather than several years old). The command word ‘Evaluate’ on a campaign question requires you to consider both strengths and limitations of a method or campaign — a one-sided answer cannot reach the top band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Named current UK campaigns include: Dry January (alcohol), No Smoking Day and Stoptober (smoking), Movember (men’s health), Time to Talk Day and Five Ways to Well-being (mental health), This Girl Can and Cycle to Work Day (physical activity), and Anti-Bullying Week (community). Always learn the campaign name, not just the theme.
  • Six delivery methods are used by campaigns: printed materials, websites, television advertising, celebrities and soap operas, social media and pop-ups, and guest speakers in schools and colleges. Each has strengths and limitations.
  • Reliable and valid health information comes from NHS bodies, registered charities, and government organisations, is underpinned by clinical evidence, is recently updated, and is appropriate for the target group. Always consider who produced the information and why.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a named UK campaign that promotes awareness of mental health?
A) Dry January
B) Movember
C) Time to Talk Day
D) No Smoking Day
practice_questions.marks: C) Time to Talk Day [1 mark]. Dry January promotes alcohol reduction; Movember promotes men's physical and mental health (accept Movember if a student argues the mental health element, but Time to Talk is the primary mental health campaign listed in the specification); No Smoking Day promotes smoking cessation.

practice_questions.text: Identify two methods that health campaigns use to reach their target audiences.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct methods from the six (max 2). Acceptable answers: printed materials such as leaflets and posters [1]; websites and online resources [1]; television advertisements [1]; celebrities, soap operas and drama [1]; social media and internet pop-ups [1]; guest speakers in schools and colleges [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why social media is used as a method of delivering health campaigns to young people.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the reason (young people use social media frequently / it reaches a large proportion of the target group); 1 mark for a developed reason using 'because' (e.g. because social media platforms allow campaigns to target specific age groups with relevant, shareable content that can spread peer to peer); 1 mark for a limitation or further development (e.g. however, misinformation also spreads rapidly on social media, so campaign messages from credible NHS or charity sources may compete with inaccurate information from unverified accounts).

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'Five Ways to Well-being' and explain one way in which a health professional could use this framework with a service user.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for accurately describing Five Ways to Well-being (a framework developed by the New Economics Foundation identifying five evidence-based actions to improve well-being: connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, and give [1]; adopted by NHS and public health bodies as a well-being promotion tool [1]). Up to 2 marks for a specific, plausible practitioner example (e.g. a community nurse working with an isolated older adult could use the 'connect' action to encourage them to join a local social group, because social connection is an evidence-based way to improve mental well-being and reduce loneliness [1]; the nurse discusses which of the five actions the service user finds most realistic given their circumstances, applying the framework in a person-centred way [1]).

practice_questions.text:
Devika is 45 years old and is looking for information online about whether she should take a particular herbal supplement that claims to reduce blood pressure. She has found two sources: one from the NHS website and one from a blog run by the supplement manufacturer.

Discuss how Devika could assess the reliability and validity of each source of information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Applies reliability and validity criteria specifically to both sources with developed reasoning. NHS website: produced by a public health body with no commercial interest in a particular product [1]; information is based on clinical evidence reviewed by medical professionals [1]; content is regularly updated, so advice reflects current guidance [1]. Supplement manufacturer's blog: commercial interest — the producer benefits financially from promoting the supplement [1]; evidence may be based on customer testimonials rather than clinical trials, which is less reliable [1]; information may not be reviewed by qualified health professionals and may be out of date or selectively presented [1]. Overall assessment: Devika should rely on the NHS source for accurate guidance on managing blood pressure; the manufacturer's source is less valid because it may not accurately reflect the full clinical picture [1].

Secure (3–4 marks): Addresses both sources with some reliability/validity analysis; at least two developed points.

Developing (2 marks): Addresses one source or gives a very general answer about reliability.

Emerging (1 mark): Identifies one source as more reliable without explanation.

practice_questions.text: Evaluate how effectively the method of using celebrities and soap opera storylines promotes health and well-being across different groups in the population.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (9–10 marks): Balanced evaluation addressing specific strengths and limitations of using celebrities and soap opera storylines as a campaign delivery method, with reference to different population groups. Strengths: reaches large audiences who do not actively seek health information — soap opera viewers include older adults, families and young people across social backgrounds; emotional storytelling can change attitudes more effectively than information alone because audiences empathise with characters; a celebrity speaking openly about mental health (e.g. a public figure discussing depression) can normalise help-seeking, particularly among groups (e.g. men) who are reluctant to admit vulnerability; evidence from mental health charities shows that soap opera storylines (e.g. suicide storylines handled responsibly) lead to increased calls to support services in the following days. Limitations: not always factually accurate — entertainment takes precedence over precision; not all groups watch television or follow specific celebrities — younger people, recent migrants and those without mainstream media access may not be reached; messages delivered indirectly through storylines may not be specific enough to enable individual action; celebrities who endorse products commercially may reduce public trust. Evaluation of effectiveness by group: effective for older adults (high soap viewing rates) and for reducing stigma around mental health (Time to Talk); less effective for reaching those not represented in mainstream media. Conclusion: celebrity and soap methods are effective for reaching broad audiences and changing attitudes, but they should be combined with targeted local delivery methods (e.g. guest speakers, social media) to reach groups underserved by mainstream media.

Secure (6–8 marks): Addresses most strengths and limitations with some group differentiation and a conclusion.

Developing (3–5 marks): Addresses some strengths and limitations; limited differentiation by group.

Emerging (1–2 marks): One-sided or very general response.

flashcard_questions.q: Which organisation runs Dry January, and when does it take place?
What health issues does Movember focus on?
flashcard_questions.a: Men's health — prostate cancer, testicular cancer and men's mental health.

flashcard_questions.q: Who runs Time to Talk Day, and what is its aim?
flashcard_questions.a: Mind and Rethink Mental Illness — encouraging open conversations about mental health to reduce stigma.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the five actions in the Five Ways to Well-being framework.
flashcard_questions.a: Connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, give.

flashcard_questions.q: What campaign runs each October to encourage smokers to quit for a month?
Name two methods used to deliver health campaigns.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two from: printed materials, websites, TV advertisements, celebrities/soap operas, social media, guest speakers.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might social media be an effective delivery method for reaching young people?
flashcard_questions.a: Young people use social media frequently and content can be shared peer to peer.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'reliable' mean when evaluating health information?
flashcard_questions.a: The information is consistent and produced by a credible organisation without a commercial interest.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'valid' mean when evaluating health information?
flashcard_questions.a: The information is accurate, based on sound evidence and appropriate to the individual's situation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is information from a supplement manufacturer's website less reliable than NHS advice?
flashcard_questions.a: The manufacturer has a commercial interest in promoting its product, not in providing impartial health advice.

flashcard_questions.q: What campaign encourages women and girls to be physically active regardless of fitness level?
What is the original name for what is now called NHS Better Health?
flashcard_questions.a: Change4Life (launched 2009, rebranded to Better Health in 2020).

glossary_terms.definition: A series of public health campaigns run by NHS England, initially launched as Change4Life in 2009, rebranded to Better Health in 2020, promoting healthy eating, physical activity and tobacco cessation.
An annual public health campaign run each January by Alcohol Change UK, encouraging people to take a month off alcohol to improve their health and raise money for charity.

An annual campaign held each November by the Movember Foundation, raising awareness of men's health issues including prostate cancer, testicular cancer and mental health, through sponsored moustache-growing and fundraising.
An annual mental health awareness day held on the first Thursday of February, run jointly by Mind and Rethink Mental Illness, encouraging open conversation about mental health to reduce stigma.

A framework developed by the New Economics Foundation (NEF) and adopted by NHS and public health bodies, identifying five evidence-based actions shown to improve well-being: connect, be active, take notice, keep learning, and give.
The consistency of information or data — a reliable source produces consistent information that other credible sources agree with.
The accuracy and appropriateness of information — valid information is truthful, based on good evidence, and relevant to the individual's specific situation.

items.title: Psychology and the Good Life | Laurie Santos | Yale
items.description: Yale professor Laurie Santos' lecture on evidence-based happiness — closely mirrors the Five Ways to Well-being framework and is highly watchable for students.

items.title: How to Motivate Yourself to Change Behaviour | Tali Sharot | TEDxCambridge
items.description: The science behind why campaigns succeed or fail at changing behaviour — directly relevant to evaluating the effectiveness of health campaign methods.

items.title: The Century of the Self (2002)
items.description: Adam Curtis' landmark BBC documentary on how mass persuasion techniques shape public attitudes — provides historical context for how health campaigns borrow from advertising to change behaviour.

items.title: NHS Better Health — Campaign Hub
items.description: The main NHS Better Health site — home to Stoptober, NHS Couch to 5K, alcohol guidance and more. Students can explore named campaigns directly from their official source.

items.title: Alcohol Change UK — Dry January
items.description: Official Dry January campaign site — includes participant resources, research evidence and campaign history for the alcohol awareness campaign named in the specification.

items.title: Sport England — This Girl Can
items.description: Official This Girl Can campaign hub with videos and evidence of impact — students can evaluate the campaign's methods and target audience as an extended-response example.

items.title: Movember Foundation — UK
items.description: Official Movember UK site explaining the men's health campaign, its evidence base and fundraising model — primary source for the named Movember campaign.

items.title: Mind — Time to Talk Day
items.description: Mind's official Time to Talk Day page — includes the campaign's aims, evidence and resources for reducing mental health stigma.

items.title: New Economics Foundation — Five Ways to Well-being
items.description: The original NEF report and evidence base for the Five Ways to Well-being framework — primary source for the specification requirement to know this framework.
